en: Udānavarga from Subaši 1. Anityavarga [Verses 1–40: lost]
... and having performed this task ... [Verse 42 lost]
2. Kāmavarga [Verses 1–8 lost] Having conceived desire, one does not flow away.
And it should become clear through the mind...
following after.
He did not attain satisfaction through the mind;
therefore, having turned away from each object of action and attained wisdom, the person becomes satisfied.
The greedy one brings himself under the power of craving. [Stanzas 16–17 lost]
The disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving,
like a mountain.
... from whatever cause he saw [it] regarding sensual pleasures...
3. The Chapter on Craving (Tṛṣṇāvarga)
... this will be abandoned; it causes the fetter to rot.
For a person who wanders about with passion, craving...
covered by the covering of craving.
The heedless are bound in bondage, like fish at the mouth of a net.
Fools, attached and bound by the fetters, encounter suffering once again for a long night.
Bound by craving... [Stanza 8 lost] ... which are so difficult to abandon.
His sorrows increase like *bīraṇa* grass drenched by rain for him who does not abandon these worldly [desires].
Like a drop of water from a lotus leaf,
dig out craving with its very roots, as many as have gathered here today.
As one seeking uśīra grass finds only vīraṇa,
so it is for one who seeks [peace] while possessed by craving;
a person has craving as his companion.
Having repeatedly taken up [existence],
one enters the womb again and again.
This state of being, the state of becoming otherwise, the coming and going of sentient beings,
and that craving...
there exists that one upon whom gods and humans rely and remain intent on their goals.
Cross over this clinging attachment...
this clinging attachment is like a spreading net that has reached the root of the boil.
Just as a creeper grows without having removed its thirst for water,
so too does one grow while the underlying tendency of craving has not been uprooted.
This suffering arises again and again,
just like a piercing arrow.
Craving leads living beings to their destruction;
having understood this danger, [one should abandon it].
Craving is the origin of suffering. One who is free from craving is without grasping.
4. The Chapter on Heedfulness.
the state of the deathless is the state of heedlessness regarding death; those who are heedful do not die.
Those who are heedless... the wise are in heedfulness;
in heedfulness...
The wise, through their exertions, touch [the goal]...
the person.
Just as one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground, so does the wise man look upon the foolish through his exertion.
...he does not trample upon one who is industrious, mindful, pure in action, and whose conduct is observed.
The fame of one who is self-restrained, living according to the Dharma, and vigilant increases.
For one training in the sage’s words of wisdom,
sorrows... [fade away].
One who possesses mindfulness should not practice inferior dharmas,
nor should one dwell in negligence.
O Increaser of the World,
there may be one for whom supreme right view exists.
Even thousands [of them] do not fall into an evil rebirth if they are devoted to heedfulness.
one guards against negligence; one should not indulge in sensual pleasures or social attachments.
For the one who is heedful and meditating attains the immovable; [the heedless], however, follows after heedlessness.
Like a lion to a lioness,
a man who is heedless and who consorts with another's wife falls into four states.
The third is hell, the fourth is the acquisition of demerit, an evil destiny,
fear for one who is already afraid, and very little pleasure.
And the king inflicts heavy punishment; ... he suffers [the consequences].
One should act immediately upon knowing what is beneficial for oneself;
one should not concern oneself with the deliberations of a cartwright.
One should proceed slowly and steadily with firm resolve,
just as a cart-driver, having entered upon a rugged path.
Like one whose axle is broken, he broods,
having thus departed from the Dharma and followed after non-Dharma.
The fool, having fallen under the power of death,
is made to play with the dice of the senses.
For those who are loud-mouthed and heedless,
their taints increase;
for them, the taints continue to grow.
Far from you...
[Verses 19–21 lost] ...a follower of the Dharma.
Having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion,
that Blessed One,
like Maghavan, has attained the goal of the ascetic life.
Having attained preeminence among the gods,
the wise praise heedfulness regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
The steadfast one,
through the attainment of his goals, remains heedful regarding other matters pertaining to the future life.
The wise one...
delights in heedfulness.
A monk who delights in heedfulness...
For those who perceive danger in negligence,
having realized the auspicious state of the cessation of conditioned formations, there is happiness.
[Verse 28 lost] The monk who delights in heedfulness [should be vigilant] toward heedlessness...
[The remainder of the chapter is lost.
5. Priyavarga [Verses 1–14 lost]
And I know myself to be dear; I shall protect [her] who has been entrusted to me.
... [the view] of oneself in some respect, and ...
of others.
Therefore, one who desires their own self should not harm another,
having made [the other] oneself.
One should not cause a man who has been living abroad for a long time to be killed,
even if he has returned from afar in safety.
... even when one who has performed meritorious deeds has departed from this world,
merits rejoice [in him].
Therefore, treat [them] like a beloved kinsman who has arrived; for this is what brings about [the fruits] of meritorious deeds for living beings.
The gods praise merit and one who practices right conduct; such a person remains irreproachable in this world.
Having passed away,
people make that which was a doer dear to them.
One becomes dear to others and acts for one's own benefit;
one is praised in this very life.
In the future life...
he becomes dear to the virtuous,
and he becomes unpleasant to the wicked.
Therefore, both the virtuous and the non-virtuous are distinct; those who are non-existent go to the hells.
6. Śīlavarga [Verses 1–2 lost] ... is burned.
He sleeps happily at night and awakens joyful.
Wisdom is established as the jewel of men,
a merit that thieves cannot steal.
Established in virtue and devoted to wakefulness, dwelling in this manner...
Day and night, unwearied,
the ardent and prudent monk is incapable of falling away.
Having seen this thus, one should always train accordingly... [verses 9–24 lost] ... [end of fragment]
... one would quickly purify the path leading to [that goal]; ... it blows against the wind.
The virtuous person wafts through all directions,
like the fragrance of tagara and sandalwood.
For this scent of tagara and sandalwood is indeed of little measure compared to the fragrance of those who possess virtuous conduct.
He blows as the supreme among the gods... for those who are liberated,
Māra finds no path.
[Stanza 30 lost] 7. Sucaritavarga: One should guard against bodily corruption.
One should be restrained in body... one should guard against mental malice as one goes about.
One should be restrained in mind,
having abandoned mental misconduct and practicing mental good conduct.
... though possessed of faults,
one should perform much wholesome action with the body...
One should perform wholesome deeds with the mind immeasurably; having performed wholesome deeds with the body, one is free from acquisitions.
For by means of speech,
he indeed attains even greater happiness than others.
Restraint of the body is good;
indeed, restraint of speech is good;
restraint of the mind is good.
Excellent is restraint in all things;
the monk who is restrained in all things is wise and well-restrained.
Always restrained in all circumstances,
they go to the imperishable state,
having gone to which one does not grieve.
Those who are non-violent go to the imperishable state;
[the others] grieve.
The sages who are indeed non-violent and always restrained in speech go to the imperishable abode.
Having gone where one does not grieve... the sages are perpetually restrained in mind.
They go to the deathless state... he who guards his speech and is well-restrained in mind does not grieve.
One should not perform unwholesome acts with the body;
one should purify these three paths of action.
One should follow the path proclaimed by the Seers.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "On Good Conduct."
8. The Chapter on Speech:
One who speaks what has not been seen goes to hell, as does one who says "I did it" after having done it, or one who says "I did not do it" after having done it.
Both of these become equal after death for one who has performed inferior actions; for indeed, of a person who is born...
An axe is born in the mouth,
by which one cuts oneself while speaking ill-spoken words.
Through that *kalī*, one finds no happiness,
even for a moment.
... of the Arbudas; that which the Noble One... [Verses 6–9 lost]
Speaking slowly and without agitation,
he speaks of the meaning and the Dharma as they have been taught.
The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme;
one should utter only that word which does not cause one's own self to burn with remorse.
And one should not harm others;
that indeed is well-spoken speech when one speaks what is pleasing to others.
For true speech is immortal;
those who speak the truth possess unsurpassed speech regarding reality, the goal, and the Dharma.
... for the sake of abandonment; he is indeed unsurpassed in speech. This is the eighth chapter on Speech. * * *
9. Chapter on Karma:
For one who has passed beyond even a single dharma, falsehood... [is not found].
If one who is immoral and unrestrained should consume the alms-food of the kingdom, it would be like consuming molten iron needles.
If you fear suffering,
whether you have already committed it or are currently committing it,
there is no liberation for you from that suffering.
Even if one were to flee by leaping up into the air, he would not find refuge there;
for he delivers [the consequences] over to others.
Having seen an evil deed here in this world,
one should not perform it oneself;
for such a person is bound by their actions.
Those men who perform an auspicious deed indeed fall into a precipice; and then...
... they plunder ... it is plundered. [Verses 10–13 are lost.]
... one practices that deed which, once performed, is good;
having performed it, ...
One who commits no harm does not experience suffering; for indeed, one comes to know the consequences of evil only in the future life.
Whatever destination belongs to those of evil deeds,
like rust arising from iron—
this concludes the ninth chapter on Action.
10. The Chapter on Faith (Śraddhāvarga): Faith, modesty, and virtue—these qualities belong to a person of noble character.
The teachers... rejoicing in the gift, by that very act he becomes... [meritorious].
Truth is indeed the sweetness among the most excellent flavors;
wisdom is the life of those whose life is wisdom.
[Verse 4 lost] Through faith one crosses the flood; through heedfulness, the ocean.
Through vigor one abandons suffering and severs all bonds,
provided one possesses faith and virtue.
Wherever he goes, there indeed he is honored.
And he attains a concentration for which these [defilements] have been utterly severed,
like the top of a palm tree cut off.
He... at night...
should not dig up water that has the smell of mud.
One seeking water should resort to a wise person as one would to a deep heart of clear,
undisturbed water.
Having abandoned that which is cool, untroubled, and pure, one should avoid that which is not serene.
One should attend upon those who are serene;
this is the tenth chapter on the group of those endowed with faith. * * *
Impermanence, craving for sensual pleasures, heedlessness regarding those who are dear,
and conduct through speech that is contrary to virtue;
Faith in action...
11. The Chapter on Ascetics:
Cut off the stream by exerting yourself.
O Brahmin, cast away sensual desires;
for without abandoning desires, a sage does not attain oneness.
Whether one succeeds or not,
one should exert firm effort;
for a mendicant who is lax is indeed a failure.
Any action that is slack,
or austerity that is defiled,
or a holy life that is impure.
A poorly grasped arrow brings no happiness, just as it does when it strikes the hand.
... if wrongly grasped, it drags one down to hell, just as an arrow [drags one down] when not well-grasped.
One does not cut off one's own hand;
the state of a recluse, when well-grasped, is indeed close to Nirvana.
The life of a recluse is difficult to practice and difficult to endure;
therein are many obstacles.
Where the dull-witted despair, how should one practice the ascetic life so as not to obstruct the mind?
Falling into despair at every step,
they have fallen under the sway of their own volitions;
[this] going forth is difficult to undertake and difficult to find joy in.
Houses are difficult to dwell in;
living together with equals is suffering;
existence is beset by suffering.
Many with saffron-colored necks are unrestrained, possessing evil qualities;
they are wicked due to their wicked deeds.
From here one goes to a miserable destiny, being utterly immoral,
like a *sāla* tree entwined by a *mālatī* creeper.
He makes himself such as his enemy wishes him to be;
yet he does not become an old man merely by that.
To the extent that the hair on the head has turned gray,
one's age is said to be fully ripened.
But he who, having cast off both merit and evil,
practices the holy life and moves about having made [the world] like a poisoned pit—
He indeed is called an elder,
not one who is merely shaven-headed...
[Stanza 14 lost].
One who acts thus is called a *śramaṇa*;
having washed away one's own impurity,
for that reason one is called a *pravrajita*.
The Chapter on Ascetics, the Eleventh. * * *
12. Mārgavarga:
By means of wisdom, [one realizes] the four noble truths...
He understands the path that shatters the thirst for existence,
[like] dust raised by the wind.
Just as it is stilled by a cloud,
so do conceptual constructions subside when one perceives with wisdom.
For wisdom is the best in the world, leading to disenchantment;
it is by means of this that one understands correctly.
The noble eightfold path is the best for seeking the destruction of birth and death;
it consists of four truths.
Dispassion is the foremost of all dharmas, and among bipeds... [it is the foremost].
"Conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
When one sees with wisdom,
then one becomes weary of suffering;
this is the path to purification.
When one perceives through wisdom that "all is impermanent and suffering," [it leads] to purification.
When one perceives through wisdom that all suffering is indeed without self,
then one becomes disenchanted with suffering.
This is the path to purification;
for all things are empty and without self.
... the path that extracts the thorn of craving ... they will abandon [it].
For one who meditates, this is the breaking of Māra’s bonds; this, moreover,
is the supreme exertion, like the path of a swan departing from a pond.
That which Śākyamuni,
who perceives the end of the destruction of birth, has repeatedly realized as the single path.
He has proclaimed the path for the benefit [of beings]:
by this path, those of old have crossed over,
those yet to come will cross over, and those who are crossing now cross the flood.
...purity for the exhaustion of birth and death in saṃsāra;
for the analytical knowledge of the manifold elements.
For this path has been revealed by the One with Vision; like the current of the Gaṅgā flowing toward the ocean,
it merges into it.
In the same way, the path taught by the one of vast wisdom flows together toward this attainment of the deathless.
By her, the Wheel of Dharma, which had not been heard before, [was turned].
Compassionate toward all beings, he shall set it forth;
such a one, O Deva...
that being, the world pays homage as one who has reached the further shore of existence.
One should contemplate the three wholesome thoughts and likewise avoid the three unwholesome ones.
Then one should pacify both applied thought and sustained thought, as rain [calms the dust],
and should bind [the mind] to the object.
Cultivate the immeasurable states born of seclusion;
[stanzas 19–20 lost].
13. Satkāravarga [Verses 1–2 lost] ... [mātsaryaṃ] (avarice)
[Verse 4 is lost] ... it increases;
for other are the means to gain.
Another leads to Nirvāṇa;
[Stanza 6 is lost] ... everywhere.
A man should not exist apart from this;
he should not live by depending on anything other than the Dharma.
[Verse 8 is lost] Well-composed in moral virtues.
[The remainder of the chapter is lost.]
The thirteenth chapter, the Section on Honor, is completed. // * //
14. Chapter on Divisiveness:
He who would do harm here to one who is not angry is a person of evil deeds...
...evil touches him;
the one who is struck down strikes back,
just as a bird is struck by a snare.
What else is there for one who reviles a reviler and provokes anger in one who provokes anger,
other than not listening?
... when being torn apart, do not consider anything weak; though the bones are shattered, the life-force...
... they bind enmity to themselves—those who... [verses 7–9 lost].
[Verse 11 lost] ... for the sake of non-enmity [Verses 13–14 lost]
While walking, one should not perceive [them];
one should act with little concern, like a coal in a forest.
The fourteenth chapter on the category of distinctions is completed. * * *
15. The Chapter on Mindfulness... taught by him;
he illuminates this world.
Like the moon released from the clouds... having attained a state of distinction...
...the mindfulness directed toward the body, established and present, would come to mind regarding the six bases of contact of the King of Death...
For one who possesses mindfulness directed toward the body, established constantly and at all times, there is Nirvana for oneself.
He who remains awake while the night is still clinging, being mindful, clearly comprehending,
composed, joyful, and serene.
Investigating the true Dharma,
one shall transcend birth...
A monk who is ardent and mindful of the Buddha,
having abandoned the fetters and birth and old age,
shall here and now make an end of suffering.
Awake, listen to this! You who were asleep, now awaken;
you who are asleep...
Fear belongs to those who sleep;
it does not belong to one who is devoted to wakefulness and trains himself day and night.
For one who has pursued the Deathless,
the taints go to their end;
this is their gain.
Those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha,
for whom [there is peace] by day and by night—
Constant mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, constant mindfulness directed toward the Dharma, and constant mindfulness directed toward the Saṅgha.
[Verse 12 lost] Constant mindfulness directed toward ethical conduct... mindfulness.
Constant mindfulness directed toward yoga leads to non-violence.
[Verses 17–21 are lost.]
The Sangha’s Meditative Absorption [Verses 24–28 lost]
For those whose mindfulness is directed toward the signless both by day and by night;
this is the fifteenth section on mindfulness. * * *
16. Prakīrṇakavarga:
Previously...
[one should] do what is to be done at the time for doing it.
One who fails to perform what ought to be done will not accomplish that task when the time for action arrives.
A person should exert effort as long as there is the accomplishment of their goal;
so do I perceive myself.
As one desires, so it shall be; arise, exert yourselves,
and practice!
Just as a smith removes the dross from silver,
so do those who are ashamed of what they should not be ashamed of purify the impurities of their own selves.
Those who are shameless regarding what should cause shame,
who see fear where there is no fear, and who see no fear where there is fear.
Those beings who go to a miserable rebirth due to falsehood...
Thereafter, he does not become negligent;
he shines forth in this world like the moon released from clouds.
Thus,
being mindful, he completely transcends this attachment to the world.
Though young... like the moon released from clouds, he illuminates the world.
Thus,
the virtuous one transcends this world of differentiation.
[Verses 9–10 lost] At the end of life he does not grieve;
he is indeed a wise man who has seen the state.
In the midst of sorrow he does not grieve; in the midst of kinsmen he shines, [practicing] the dark dharmas...
Having abandoned sensual desires, one who possesses nothing should seek delight therein; for,
O Phalguna, it is always the fruit of purity.
For one who is pure, the *poṣadha* is always [fulfilled];
for one whose actions are clean,
the vow is constantly accomplished.
fields are these beings, characterized by passion and hatred;
[but for one] who is free from passion...
A gift given [to such a person] yields great fruit;
fields have defects of weeds,
but this is the nature of living beings.
Therefore, a gift given to one who is free from faults yields great fruit;
thus it is with delusion.
The fault of pride,
the fault of craving,
and the sixth, the sovereign king.
One who is being colored is "possessed of passion" (*rajasvala*);
for one who is not colored is called a fool.
The city has a wall of bones and a plastering of flesh and blood,
wherein reside both passion and hatred.
Conceit and hypocrisy plunge ever deeper into the origin of causes;
through the clear realization of that [origin], they are abandoned.
For outsiders do not abandon those attachments,
Ghoṭamukha.
The sixteenth chapter, the Miscellaneous Section, is completed. * //
17. The Chapter on Water:
Those possessed of mindfulness do not delight in a dwelling.
Like swans leaving a pond, those swans abandon flood after flood along the path of the sun.
In the midst of space...
having neither practiced the holy life nor acquired wealth in one's youth.
They meditate like a withered crane, or they lie like small fish in a shallow pool, or scattered like arrows.
Remembering these ancient [teachings],
he will come; by the falling of drops of water...
Just as a large jar is filled by being poured bit by bit,
so too is a fool filled with evil by accumulating it little by little.
One should not think lightly of merit,
[believing] "it will not come to me," for it accumulates by the falling of drops of water.
is filled; the wise are filled with merit... of those who accumulate [it].
Those who cross the ocean-like lake abandon the small ponds;
for people indeed construct a raft.
The wise have crossed over... what could the disciples do with a well?
And water would exist everywhere;
having cut off the root of craving here in this world, for whom [would thirst remain]?
Just as carpenters bend wood by means of fire,
so do the wise bend themselves.
Just as a lake [is not defiled by mud], so too is such a person of noble character, like a pillar of Indra, unstained.
Like lakes from which the mud has been removed, [are] the cycles of existence...
[the Chapter on Water, the seventeenth]. * * *
18. The Chapter on Flowers:
Who will investigate this earth, and this world of Yama together with its gods?
Who, being skillful, will select the well-taught word of the Dharma like a flower?
He, being skilled, will select from this world of Yama and the world of the gods the well-taught verse of Dharma,
just as one would choose a flower.
Cut down the forest, not the tree;
from the forest fear is born. And [cut down] the forest...
Become extinguished, O monks,
as long as even the slightest bit of forest— the attachment to one's kinsmen— is not cut down within a person.
For one whose mind is bound by affection, my dear child, cuts off his own love just as a suckling calf tears away from its mother.
Like an autumnal lotus with the hand,
one should cultivate only the path of peace—
the Nirvana taught by the Sugata.
Just as a beautiful flower, possessing color...
[and] fruit... [is pleasing].
Just as a beautiful flower that is colorful and fragrant, so too... [is the person who speaks well but does not act].
Just as a sage in a village takes away only the flavor [of what he needs],
so too [he does not take] the hair of others against their will.
Just as a lotus might grow upon a heap of refuse cast away on the great highway.
Pure in scent and delightful to the mind;
even so [is it] within this blind heap of refuse.
The disciple of the Perfectly Awakened One is pleasing to the people,
just as [a tree] is with heaps of flowers.
Just as one would make many strands for a garland,
so too should a mortal who has been born perform much that is wholesome.
Just as the autumnal [lotus] sheds its petals,
so too does it cast off passion and hatred.
O monks, release [your minds];
do not let men here, while gathering flowers, have their minds distracted.
Death departs, taking away a sleeping village and a man whose mind is distracted.
Like a great flood sweeping away a sleeping village, death carries one away while they remain unsated in their desires.
Having cut through the flower-bow of Māra here in this world, [one should avoid] a person whose mind is distracted regarding things that have not yet arisen...
O world, who indeed would go to the state of being unseen by the King of Death?
Having understood this body to be like foam, and having fully awakened to its nature as a mirage—
Having cut off the flowers of Māra here on earth, one should dwell [in peace].
The non-perception of the King of Death is like this in the world:
it is as rare as the flower of the udumbara tree.
That monk abandons this shore and the further shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin,
he who has cut off passion without remainder.
Like one who has plunged into the water and gathered a lotus flower,
that monk...
...just as one casts off old, worn-out skin,
so too [one casts off] the delusion of the defilements.
The eighteenth chapter, the section on Pride and Craving, is completed. // * //
19. The Chapter on Horses (Aśvavarga):
Just as a noble horse, when touched by the whip, [exerts itself] in the heat of the sun...
Possessing faith and ethical discipline, as well as vigor, meditative concentration, and the discernment of phenomena.
Those who possess perfected knowledge and conduct, who are mindful,
ardent, and self-controlled as they practice, will abandon all states of existence.
Possessing faith, virtue, and likewise vigor, concentration, and the discernment of the Dharma,
they are composed in patience, gentleness, and mental composure.
The [faculties] of one who has heard [the Dharma] have reached equanimity, like a well-tamed horse guided by a charioteer.
Even the gods envy such a person who has abandoned anger, who is free from outflows,
and who is heedful among the heedless.
Like those who leave behind weak horses, the wise depart; the man who dwells with the bold is truly successful.
The wise one, well-composed,
casts off all evils,
just as a noble horse shakes off the whip.
Tamed... tamed is the best among humans: he who endures harsh speech.
One who would tame a mule, or a well-bred Sindhava horse,
or a great elephant, a noble tusker.
Therefore, there is no better taming than the taming of oneself;
for by means of a well-tamed self, [one attains peace].
The tamed one goes with the tamed; one should tame oneself alone, just as a skilled charioteer tames a noble horse.
For the self, when tamed by oneself,
is mindful and reaches the further shore of suffering; it is one's own refuge.
Therefore, restrain yourself as a merchant restrains a noble horse.
This concludes the nineteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Horses."
20. The Chapter on Anger: One should abandon anger; one should utterly abandon pride.
He would transcend all fetters,
not clinging to name-and-form.
Attachments do not pursue one who possesses nothing;
one should abandon anger as soon as it arises and restrain passion once it has been born.
The wise one should abandon ignorance through the clear realization of the truths, having slain anger with ease.
... he grieves,
O Brahmin, for anger which has poison as its root and strikes at what is sweet.
The noble ones praise killing;
having slain him, one does not grieve.
One becomes shameless, devoid of dread of blame, lacking in moral conduct, and prone to anger; for one who is overcome by anger.
There is no island whatsoever that can serve as a refuge for one who is powerful.
It is the weak who endure;
he who, though being a master over others, is himself weak, is one who endures.
The strong person endures;
that is called the supreme patience.
The weak person always forgives.
Having recognized that both oneself and others have become greatly agitated...
The steadfast one becomes pacified therein by himself; even when severely reviled, he remains patient.
They call that the supreme patience: when one who is weak always forgives, [attaining] the welfare of both.
And for oneself... and:
he who, knowing another to be angry, himself becomes calm in that situation.
One who is free from anger, truthful in speech,
and gives even a little when asked—
by these three qualities...
One should go into the presence of the gods and speak words free from anger in assemblies, O Māriṣa.
A person overcome by anger does not perceive his own welfare;
it results only in his own misfortune.
He who returns anger with anger conquers a battle difficult to win.
One should conquer anger with non-anger;
one should conquer the wicked with goodness;
one should conquer the miserly with generosity.
Truth [prevails] over untruth; the anger of one who is not angry prevails over the anger of one who is subdued.
... and non-violence always dwells among the noble ones;
then...
People who grasp at [wrong] views enter the category of anger.
The ascetic [should cultivate] respect for the path, mindfulness of the divisions [of the teachings], miscellaneous [practices],
and [the overcoming of] anger.
21. The Chapter on the Tathāgata: "I am all-knowing regarding all phenomena, and I am unsullied by them."
Having abandoned all [taints] through the destruction of craving, liberated by myself through direct knowledge, whom should I point to?
Whom should I point out as superior, I who am peerless, having myself attained the awakening that is to be reached?
For I am indeed the Worthy One in the world;
